title: Priests, Kings, and the Sickness Assyria Cannot Heal
summary: The LORD summons the priests, the people, and the royal house to judgment, for they have been a snare to Israel and have turned to prostitution. Their deeds keep them from returning, and when they bring flocks and herds to seek him, he has withdrawn. An alarm sounds in the towns of Benjamin as war comes; Ephraim and Judah, sick and wounded, turn to the king of Assyria, but God himself is the moth, the rot, and the lion, and he will withdraw until they admit their guilt and seek his face.
story: Chapter 4 put the priests on trial. Chapter 5 widens the circle to include the king's household and brings Judah into the indictment alongside Israel. The mood darkens from the corruption of worship to the consequences of it: war, invasion, and a failed search for help from the rising power of Assyria. The chapter ends with God withdrawing to his place, waiting for Israel to seek him, and that sets up the call to return that opens chapter 6. The two chapters belong together, and many readers treat 5:8 to 6:6 as a single unit.
historical:
Verses 8-15 most likely reflect the crisis known as the Syro-Ephraimite war, about 734 to 732 BC. Pekah king of Israel and Rezin king of Damascus tried to force Judah into an alliance against Assyria, attacked Jerusalem, and aimed to replace King Ahaz (2 Kings 16:5; Isaiah 7:1-6). Ahaz appealed to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III, who crushed Damascus, took Galilee and Gilead from Israel, and left Pekah with a shrunken kingdom (2 Kings 15:29; 16:7-9). The German scholar Albrecht Alt proposed that the alarm sounded at Gibeah, Ramah, and Beth-aven (verse 8), towns in Benjamin on the road north from Jerusalem, describes Judah's counterattack into Israelite territory, and that the princes of Judah who move boundary stones (verse 10) are Judah seizing land. Many scholars have followed this reading, though others place the passage more generally in the turmoil of the period.

Both kingdoms turned to Assyria. Menahem of Israel had paid heavy tribute to secure his throne (2 Kings 15:19-20), and Ahaz of Judah sent silver and gold from the temple to buy Assyrian help (2 Kings 16:8). Hosea's verdict is that the great king cannot cure them. Assyria eventually swallowed the northern kingdom and reduced Judah to a vassal.
cultural:
Mizpah and Tabor (verse 1) were probably sites of worship or royal administration; Mount Tabor rises from the Jezreel Valley, and there were several places called Mizpah (watchtower). The images of snare and net come from the bird-catcher's trade: the leaders who should have protected the people trapped them instead. Blowing the ram's horn (shofar) and trumpet sounded the alarm of invasion from town to town.

Moving a boundary stone was a serious crime in Israel, because land was the family's inheritance from God and markers were easy to shift at night (Deuteronomy 19:14; 27:17; Proverbs 22:28). The New Moon (verse 7) was a monthly festival; Hosea turns it into a picture of judgment, as if the festival itself will consume them. The great king (verse 13) matches a title Assyrian rulers used for themselves, and the Hebrew phrase may be a wordplay meaning a king who picks a fight.
literary: The chapter is a set of short, linked oracles. It opens with a threefold summons (hear, take heed, give ear) addressed to priests, people, and royal house. Verses 8-15 are shaped like a war alarm and then a diagnosis. Hosea uses shocking images for God. First he is like a moth and like decay or rot, slow and hidden destruction eating away from inside (verse 12). Then he is like a lion that tears its prey and carries it off (verse 14). The movement from slow decay to sudden violence matches the history: long moral rot, then Assyrian invasion. The last verse is quieter: God returns to his place and waits. Its final words, they will earnestly seek Me, lead straight into the people's song in 6:1-3.

outline.t: A summons to priests, people, and royal house
A spirit of prostitution: they seek but do not find
The alarm sounds: judgment on Ephraim and Judah
Assyria cannot heal; God withdraws until they seek him

doctrines.note: Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God (verse 4). Sin is not only a list of acts but a condition that binds people, a spirit of prostitution within them that makes turning back impossible on their own.
Turning to Assyria for healing is treated as the same kind of sin as turning to Baal. Trusting a political power for what only God can give is idolatry in another form.
God himself is the moth, the rot, and the lion. The disasters that come on Israel are not random; they are God's hand, and his withdrawal is itself a judgment.
God withdraws until they admit their guilt and seek his face (verse 15). His absence is purposeful: it is meant to drive them to real confession rather than to more sacrifices or alliances.

words.note: Rapha, to heal. Assyria cannot heal Israel's wound (verse 13); only God can, as the next chapter confesses: He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us (6:1). Hosea uses the word often, and 14:4 ends with God's promise to heal their apostasy.

Baqash, to seek. The people go with their flocks and herds to seek the LORD, but they do not find him (verse 6), because they bring sacrifices without repentance. In verse 15 God waits for a different kind of seeking, one that admits guilt.

Ash, a moth, the insect that silently eats cloth. The image is of slow, unseen destruction. God compares himself to it, a startling picture that shows how judgment can work from within long before it is visible.

christ: The chapter's diagnosis, a sickness no human power can heal, prepares for the Bible's hope in the God who heals. Jesus described his mission in exactly these terms: it is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick (Matthew 9:12), a saying he immediately joined to a quotation from Hosea 6:6. The pattern of God withdrawing until his people seek his face also shapes the New Testament's call to repentance, and the God who tears and then heals in Hosea is revealed most fully at the cross, where Isaiah's words are applied to Christ: by his wounds we are healed (1 Peter 2:24, drawing on Isaiah 53:5). The link is thematic: Hosea does not predict Jesus here, but he names the disease that only God's own remedy can cure.

hard.q: How can God describe himself as rot and as a lion tearing its prey?
hard.a:
The images are deliberately disturbing. Israel had come to think of the LORD as a safe presence at its shrines, one god among the powers it could manage with sacrifices. Hosea shatters that picture. The God of the covenant is not tame, and when his people betray him, the covenant's own warnings come into force (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28). The lion image appears elsewhere in the prophets for God's judgment (Amos 3:8; Hosea 13:7-8), and Israel would experience it historically through Assyria's armies.

Two things keep the image from being the whole picture. First, God says he will tear them and then go away to his place until they seek him; the purpose is return, not annihilation. Second, the very next verses, whether read as sincere repentance or shallow hope, confess that the God who tears is also the God who heals (6:1). Readers differ on how to relate God's anger and his love, but Hosea insists on both, and refuses to let either cancel the other.

questions: Israel brought sacrifices but did not find God. How is it possible to go through the motions of worship while God is absent?
Ephraim saw his sickness and turned to Assyria rather than God. Where are you tempted to look for healing from something that cannot provide it?
God withdraws until his people admit their guilt. Why might confession be the doorway back to God's presence?
